content: Strategies to reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV include lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV-positive women, exclusive breastfeeding for six weeks combined with nevirapine or replacement feeding with nevirapine for four to six weeks, elective Caesarean section delivery, and avoiding the practice of giving children chewed food. However, in certain settings, these interventions may not be practical, feasible, or affordable. Therefore, simple, low-cost, and effective interventions that could be implemented even in the absence of prenatal HIV testing programs are of significant interest. Vitamin A, known for its role in immune function, has been proposed as one such low-cost intervention. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of vitamin A supplementation in HIV-positive women during pregnancy and after delivery. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, Embase, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) up to August 25, 2017. Reference lists of relevant articles were also reviewed to identify eligible studies. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing vitamin A supplementation to placebo or no intervention in HIV-positive women during pregnancy, after delivery, or both. Five trials met the inclusion criteria. These trials were conducted in Malawi, South Africa, Tanzania, and Zimbabwe between 1995 and 2005, a period during which none of the participants received ART. Women in the intervention groups received vitamin A supplements in varying regimens, such as daily doses during pregnancy, a single dose immediately after delivery, or a combination of both. Women in the comparison groups received either identical placebos (in four trials involving 6601 women) or no intervention (in one trial involving 697 women). Four trials (involving 6995 women) were assessed as having a low risk of bias, while one trial (involving 303 women) had a high risk of attrition bias. The findings suggest that vitamin A supplementation during pregnancy, the immediate postpartum period, or both, likely has little or no effect on the risk of mother-to-child transmission of HIV (risk ratio [RR] 1.07, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91 to 1.26; moderate-certainty evidence from 4428 women across five trials). Similarly, vitamin A supplementation may have little or no effect on child mortality by two years of age (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.22; low-certainty evidence from 3883 women across three trials). However, vitamin A supplementation during pregnancy may increase the mean birthweight (mean difference [MD] 34.12 g, 95% CI −12.79 to 81.02; low-certainty evidence from 2181 women across three trials) and probably reduces the incidence of low birthweight (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.97; moderate-certainty evidence from 1819 women across three trials). The evidence is insufficient to determine whether vitamin A supplementation affects the risk of preterm delivery (1577 women across two trials), stillbirth (2335 women across three trials), or maternal death (1267 women across two trials). In conclusion, vitamin A supplementation during pregnancy or the postpartum period likely has little or no effect on mother-to-child transmission of HIV in women living with HIV who are not receiving ART. While it may have some benefits in terms of birthweight, its role in preventing vertical transmission of HIV has been largely superseded by the widespread availability and effectiveness of ART.
